title: The missed morning flight
prompt: Tell a friend how you missed an early flight. What went wrong, and what did you do next?
beats: Set the scene: the plan and the morning itself
The moment it turned: when you knew it was gone
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: My flight to Pune was at six, so I set two alarms. But I set both for 6 p.m., not 6 a.m. That was the oversight. I woke up at 5:40 to my mum calling. So I rebooked on the noon flight, paid the fee and spent a hectic morning explaining it to my team. Now I check a.m. and p.m. twice.

title: The bike skid in the rain
prompt: Tell a friend about the time your bike skidded on a wet road. What happened exactly?
beats: Set the scene: where you were and the weather
The moment it turned: the skid itself
How it ended and how you felt after

skill.answer: I was riding home from work in the first rain of the season, going slowly near the flyover. But the road was oily, and when I braked, the back wheel started to wobble and then skid. I went down on my side. So I sat on the kerb for ten minutes, shaken but fine, with just a torn sleeve. I've ridden more slowly in the rain ever since.

title: The landlord mix-up
prompt: Tell a friend about a funny misunderstanding with your landlord. What did each of you think?
beats: Set the scene: what the confusion was about
The moment it turned: when you both realised
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: My landlord texted, 'Please clear the terrace by Sunday.' It was a bit ambiguous, but I thought he meant my plants, so I spent Saturday carrying twenty pots down three floors. But on Sunday he came up and asked where my plants had gone. He'd meant the old furniture the last tenant left. It was awkward for a second. So we laughed, sorted it out, and carried the pots back up together.

title: The wrong order at lunch
prompt: Tell a friend about a time you were served completely the wrong food. What did you do?
beats: Set the scene: the place and who you were with
The moment it turned: the wrong plate arriving
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: We were at a busy South Indian place near the office, and I'd ordered a plain dosa. But the waiter put down a huge plate of chole bhature. I almost started eating before I noticed. So I flagged it, he apologised for the mix-up, and my friend ate the chole while we waited. We laughed it off, and my dosa came ten minutes later.

title: Stuck in a monsoon jam
prompt: Tell a friend about the worst traffic jam you were ever stuck in. What was it like?
beats: Set the scene: where you were headed and the rain
The moment it turned: when you knew you were stuck
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: It was a Friday evening in July, and I'd left the office at six to catch a movie. But the rain hit hard, and Outer Ring Road turned into total gridlock. We moved at a crawl, maybe one kilometre an hour. By nine, the cab driver and I were both restless and sharing my biscuits. So I missed the movie and reached home at ten. Now I check the weather before I make Friday plans.

title: The ATM that ate my card
prompt: Tell a friend about the time an ATM swallowed your card. What happened step by step?
beats: Set the scene: when and where you needed cash
The moment it turned: the machine going silent
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I was at an ATM late at night, taking out cash for my rent. But the machine froze and kept my card. I felt a wave of panic, so I called the bank's helpline right there. They blocked the card in two minutes and said a new one would take a week. So I waited it out with UPI and borrowed some cash from my flatmate.

title: Locked out of my own flat
prompt: Tell a friend about getting locked out of your own house. How did you get back in?
beats: Set the scene: how it happened
The moment it turned: realising no key, no help nearby
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I stepped out to take the rubbish down at eleven at night, and the door shut behind me. Keys inside, phone inside. I was stranded on the stairs in my shorts. But my neighbour Arjun heard me and lent me his phone. So I called my landlord, who came with a spare key at midnight. Lesson learnt: Arjun now keeps a spare key for me.

title: The wrong bus to nowhere
prompt: Tell a friend about boarding the wrong bus or train. When did you realise?
beats: Set the scene: where you meant to go
The moment it turned: spotting the wrong route
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I got on the bus after a long day, put my headphones on and dozed off. But when I woke up, the shops outside looked completely new. It was the wrong bus, going the other way. So I got off, took an auto back, and turned a twenty-minute ride into a ninety-minute detour. My flatmates still laugh about it, and honestly, so do I.

title: The phone call on speaker
prompt: Tell a friend about a time you said something awkward not knowing the phone was on speaker.
beats: Set the scene: who was on the call
The moment it turned: when you found out
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: My cousin called me during her family lunch. Thinking it was just the two of us, I blurted out, 'Is Aunty still telling the same story?' But her phone was on speaker, and Aunty was sitting right next to her. Total silence. I tried to cover it up with a joke, and it didn't work. So I called Aunty that evening, still mortified, and said sorry properly.

title: The bill that made no sense
prompt: Tell a friend about a shop bill that was clearly wrong. How did you sort it out?
beats: Set the scene: the shop and what you bought
The moment it turned: spotting the wrong charge
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I bought groceries at the supermarket, and the bill felt high. So I checked the receipt in the car park and found they'd charged me for three packs of almonds, not one. I went back in, but the cashier said the system is never wrong. I stood my ground, calmly showed her the receipt and my bag, and the manager fixed the discrepancy in two minutes. Now I check before I leave the counter.

title: The fever before the trip
prompt: Tell a friend about falling sick right before something important. What did you do?
beats: Set the scene: the plan you were excited about
The moment it turned: the fever hitting
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: We'd planned a Goa trip with college friends for six months. But two days before, I woke up with a high fever and felt completely drained. I waited a day, hoping it would pass, but it didn't. So I had to cancel, and I was gutted watching their photos from my bed. The good news: they've saved me a seat for the December trip.

title: The wedding speech scare
prompt: Tell a friend about being asked to say a few words at a wedding with zero notice.
beats: Set the scene: whose wedding and where you sat
The moment it turned: your name being called
How it ended and how you felt after

skill.answer: At my friend Rahul's wedding, I was happily eating when his dad handed me the mic and said, 'Say a few words.' I was totally rattled; I had nothing ready. So I winged it and told one story: Rahul getting lost on our college trip and asking a cow for directions. Everyone laughed, Rahul went red, and I sat down with huge relief.

title: Reply-all gone wrong
prompt: Tell a friend about a message you sent to the wrong person or group. What happened?
beats: Set the scene: what you meant to send and to whom
The moment it turned: hitting send and realising
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I meant to send my friend a meme about long meetings. But I sent it to the team group, right before our long meeting. I tried to unsend it, but my manager had already seen it. So I did some quick damage control and wrote, 'Wrong chat, but sadly accurate.' She replied with a laughing emoji. I still cringe when I think about it.

title: The dish I completely burnt
prompt: Tell a friend about a time you tried cooking something and it went badly wrong.
beats: Set the scene: what you tried to cook and for whom
The moment it turned: the smell of burning
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I wanted to surprise my parents with paneer tikka on their anniversary. But I put the tray in the oven and went to take a call. Twenty minutes later, the kitchen was full of smoke, and the paneer was charred black. So we opened every window, laughed, and ordered in from their favourite place. Mum still calls it the best anniversary dinner I never made.

title: The interview question freeze
prompt: Tell a friend about blanking out on a question in an interview. How did you recover?
beats: Set the scene: the interview and the role
The moment it turned: your mind going blank
How it ended and how you felt after

skill.answer: In my second interview round, the panel asked me to explain a project from my CV. But I blanked out completely; I couldn't remember a single detail. So I said, 'Give me a moment to pick the best example,' and took a breath to buy time. Then I started with the result, and the details came back. I recovered, and a week later I got the offer.

title: The blackout during the match
prompt: Tell a friend about a power cut at the worst possible moment. What did everyone do?
beats: Set the scene: what everyone was watching or doing
The moment it turned: the lights going out
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: It was the last over of the final, and the whole family was around the TV. But just as the bowler ran in, the power went out. The whole building let out one big groan. So my dad lit candles, my cousin found the score on his phone, and we waited it out, all crowded around one tiny screen. We won, and we cheered in the dark.

title: The midnight water leak
prompt: Tell a friend about water leaking into your flat late at night. What did you do first?
beats: Set the scene: the time and the first sign
The moment it turned: finding the source
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: At two in the morning, I woke up to a strange sound: water dripping from the ceiling onto my bed. The flat upstairs had a burst pipe. But nobody upstairs was answering the door. So I put a bucket under the leak, moved my laptop and called the landlord, who woke them up. By three, the dripping stopped, and I slept on the sofa.

title: The train I nearly missed
prompt: Tell a friend about a train you nearly missed. What saved you?
beats: Set the scene: the station and the plan
The moment it turned: realising the time
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: My train to Chennai was at 6:10, but my cab got stuck behind a wedding procession. I reached the station at 6:07. So I made a mad dash with my bag to platform five, up the stairs and down again. The train was already moving. But a guard held the door open, and I jumped in. It was sheer luck, and I've left an hour early ever since.

title: Mistaken for someone else
prompt: Tell a friend about being mistaken for a stranger, or mistaking one yourself. What happened?
beats: Set the scene: where it happened
The moment it turned: the awkward recognition
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I was at a café when I saw my old classmate Riya at the counter. So I walked up, tapped her shoulder and said, 'Riya! It's been years!' But she turned around, and it wasn't Riya at all. She did a double take, and I apologised about five times. Then she smiled and said, 'I get that a lot.' We both laughed it off.

title: The demo that broke live
prompt: Tell a friend about a demo or video call that broke in front of important people.
beats: Set the scene: who was watching
The moment it turned: the thing breaking
How it ended and how you felt after

skill.answer: I was showing our new dashboard to the client's leadership on a video call. But right on the main screen, a glitch made every chart go blank. My heart was racing, but I kept my composure. So I said, 'Let me show you the version I tested this morning,' and used a recorded walkthrough as a workaround. We fixed the bug that evening, and the client approved it the next week.

title: Bargaining gone too far
prompt: Tell a friend about a time you bargained hard at a market. Did it work out?
beats: Set the scene: the shop and the price quoted
The moment it turned: the final offer
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: At a market in Jaipur, I liked a cotton bedsheet, and the seller quoted two thousand rupees. I offered six hundred, sure he'd meet me halfway. But he just smiled and folded it away. So I tried the oldest trick and walked away slowly. He didn't call me back. Ten minutes later, I went back and paid fifteen hundred. Not my best deal, but a great bedsheet.

title: The dog that followed me home
prompt: Tell a friend about a stray animal that followed you, or a pet doing something funny.
beats: Set the scene: where you met the animal
The moment it turned: it deciding to follow you
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: One night I bought a packet of biscuits on my way home and gave one to a stray near the shop. But she didn't stop at one. She trailed a few steps behind me all the way to my gate. So I sat on the step and fed her the rest. Now she waits there every evening, and the whole building has a soft spot for her.

title: Studying the wrong chapter
prompt: Tell a friend about preparing hard for the wrong thing before an exam or review.
beats: Set the scene: what you prepared
The moment it turned: seeing the actual paper or agenda
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: Before my third-year exam, I studied chapter seven for two full days. But when the paper came, half the questions were from chapter eight. I got that sinking feeling right away. So I answered what I could, winged the rest with common sense, and scraped through with a pass. Since then, I always check the syllabus twice.

title: Caught without an umbrella
prompt: Tell a friend about getting caught in sudden rain with no shelter. What did you do?
beats: Set the scene: the sky before it broke
The moment it turned: the downpour starting
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I'd gone to buy vegetables on a sunny Sunday, without an umbrella. But on the way back, the sky turned dark, and a heavy downpour started in seconds. The only place to take shelter was a tiny bus stop that was already full. So I just walked home and got completely drenched, vegetables and all. My mum laughed and made me ginger tea.

title: The hotel room surprise
prompt: Tell a friend about checking into a room that was nothing like the photos. What did you do?
beats: Set the scene: the booking and the arrival
The moment it turned: opening the door
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: For our Munnar trip, I booked a hotel with photos of a big room and a valley view. But the room we got was cramped and stuffy, and the window faced a wall. So I went down to reception and politely asked for a change. They moved us to the top floor at no extra cost. The view was so good that we had breakfast on the balcony every day.

title: The surprise guest at dinner
prompt: Tell a friend about unexpected guests arriving right at dinner time. How did the house react?
beats: Set the scene: the quiet evening plan
The moment it turned: the doorbell ringing
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: We'd just sat down to dinner when the doorbell rang. It was my dad's old friend with his whole family, six people. But we only had dal and rice for four. So everyone scrambled: Mum stretched the dal, I ran out for rotis, and my sister made a quick salad. It was crowded and noisy, but the warmth in that room is what I remember.

title: The match I almost skipped
prompt: Tell a friend about a game you nearly didn't watch that turned into something special.
beats: Set the scene: why you almost skipped it
The moment it turned: the play that pulled you in
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I almost skipped the IPL match my friends were watching; I was tired and wanted to tune out. But they dragged me along. With two overs left, our team needed thirty runs, and we were on the edge of our seats. Then the last ball went for six. We jumped so high we nearly broke the sofa. I'm so glad I went.

title: A stranger who helped me
prompt: Tell a friend about a stranger who helped you when you were stuck. What did they do?
beats: Set the scene: the trouble you were in
The moment it turned: the stranger stepping in
How it ended and how you felt about it

skill.answer: I was driving back from Mysore when a tyre went flat on an empty highway. My spare was flat too, and my phone was at five percent. I was stranded. But a truck driver stopped, rolled the tyre to a puncture shop two kilometres away and came back with it fixed. He refused any money. I'm still grateful, so I try to pay it forward when I see someone stuck.

title: Monday status in 30 seconds
prompt: Give your manager a 30-second update: what you finished, what is next, and what is stuck.
beats: The headline first: where things stand
The reason: what moved and what blocked you
The ask or next step: what happens this week

skill.answer: Quick update: the login page is shipped and has been live since Friday. Next is the payment screen, and that's on track for Thursday. One thing is blocked: I still need API access from the vendor. Could you nudge their lead today?

title: Pushing back on a deadline
prompt: Tell your manager the Friday deadline is not realistic. Be polite, give a reason and an option.
beats: The headline first: the date is at risk
The reason: what the work actually needs
The ask or next step: your proposed date or scope cut

skill.answer: I don't think Friday is realistic for the full report. The data cleaning alone needs three more days. I'd propose two options: the summary by Friday and the full report next Wednesday, or everything on Wednesday. Which trade-off works better for you?

title: Disagreeing with a senior
prompt: Disagree politely with a senior's plan in a meeting. Respect first, then your view.
beats: The headline first: agree on the goal, differ on the way
The reason: the risk or cost you see
The ask or next step: your alternative and a check

skill.answer: I agree we need to launch before the holidays. My one concern is launching in every city at once: if something breaks, support can't keep up. Can I suggest an alternative? We start with two cities next week and add the rest if the numbers hold.

title: Asking a busy teammate
prompt: Ask a busy teammate for help on something stuck. Keep it short and make it easy to say yes.
beats: The headline first: exactly what you need
The reason: what you already tried
The ask or next step: ten minutes and when

skill.answer: Hi Priya, I know you're busy. I'm stuck on the test server login, and you set it up. Could you give me ten minutes after lunch to unblock it? If today's bad, tomorrow morning works too.

title: Sharing bad news early
prompt: Tell your manager something slipped before they hear it elsewhere. Own it and bring a plan.
beats: The headline first: what slipped, in one line
The reason: what caused it, no excuses
The ask or next step: your fix and the new date

skill.answer: I want to flag something before you hear it from the client. I missed one of their changes in Monday's file, so the report they got was wrong. That's my oversight, and I own it. I've already fixed it, and I'll send the corrected version by four with a short note. I've also added a check so it doesn't happen again.

title: Asking for two days off
prompt: Ask your manager for two days off next week. Show that the work is covered.
beats: The headline first: the dates you need
The reason: cover arranged and nothing critical
The ask or next step: confirm and hand over

skill.answer: Could I take next Thursday and Friday off? Nothing is due on those days, and I'll hand over the client emails to Arjun on Wednesday. He's agreed to cover. If you approve it, I'll block my calendar today.

title: Client asks for more scope
prompt: The client wants extra work in the same deadline. Push back politely with an option.
beats: The headline first: what fits and what does not
The reason: the cost to the current date
The ask or next step: phased option or new date

skill.answer: We'd love to add the reports, but not by the same deadline without risking quality. The implication is a two-week delay for everything. Here's an option: we launch the agreed scope on the 30th and deliver the reports as phase two by the middle of next month. Would that work for you?

title: Asking for feedback
prompt: Ask your manager for honest feedback on your last month. Make it easy to be candid.
beats: The headline first: you want one thing to improve
The reason: where you felt unsure
The ask or next step: one habit to change

skill.answer: Could you give me ten minutes of honest feedback on my last month? I really want to improve, so please be candid. If there's one thing I'm not seeing, a blind spot, that's what I most want to hear.

title: Handing work over cleanly
prompt: Hand over your task before a holiday. State what is done, what is pending, and who to call.
beats: The headline first: the state of the work
The reason: pending items and their owners
The ask or next step: where the notes live

skill.answer: Here's where things stand before my leave. The vendor contract is done and signed. Two things are pending: the March invoices and the client's comments on the deck. Rahul is the owner for both while I'm away, and my notes are in the shared folder. For anything urgent, please call him first.

title: Saying no to a meeting
prompt: Decline a meeting that needs no input from you. Be warm, brief, and offer an alternative.
beats: The headline first: you will skip, with thanks
The reason: no open point needs you
The ask or next step: notes or a short catch-up

skill.answer: Thanks for including me. I'll skip this one, since the agenda doesn't need input from my side. Could someone share the notes afterwards? And if a question for my team comes up, please loop me in, and I'll reply the same day.

title: Giving an estimate
prompt: Give an estimate you are not fully sure of. State the range and what could change it.
beats: The headline first: the range, not one number
The reason: the two biggest unknowns
The ask or next step: when you will confirm

skill.answer: My ballpark estimate is two to three weeks. The big unknown is the old payment code; I haven't opened it yet. If it's clean, it's two weeks; if not, three. I'll confirm a firm date by Wednesday, once I've looked.

title: Reporting a production issue
prompt: Report a live issue on a call. State impact first, then cause, then the fix in progress.
beats: The headline first: who is affected and how badly
The reason: what you know so far
The ask or next step: the fix and next update time

skill.answer: Impact first: since 10:15, about a third of our users can't log in on Android. The cause looks like this morning's app update. We're mitigating it now by rolling the update back, which should take twenty minutes. I'll send an update at eleven, or sooner if it's fixed.

title: Two owners, one task
prompt: Two people think the other owns a task. Raise it calmly and propose one clear owner.
beats: The headline first: the gap, without blame
The reason: how the confusion happened
The ask or next step: one owner and a date

skill.answer: I think we have a gap on the vendor follow-up. Rahul and I both thought the other one had it, so nobody has sent it. Let's clarify now: I'll be the owner and send it today. Rahul, could you review it before it goes out?

title: Thanking someone properly
prompt: Thank a colleague who stayed late to help you. Name exactly what they did and its effect.
beats: The headline first: what they did
The reason: why it mattered to the outcome
The ask or next step: return the favour

skill.answer: Arjun, I'm really grateful you stayed late on Tuesday. You found the bug in the export, and that's why the client got their report on time. It made the difference. I've told our manager, and I'll give you the credit in Friday's review.

title: Apologising for a delay
prompt: Apologise to the team for your delay. Keep it short, own it fully, and state the new date.
beats: The headline first: the apology in one line
The reason: what happened, briefly
The ask or next step: the new date you will meet

skill.answer: I want to acknowledge the delay on the test plan. That's my miss: I underestimated the review time. The new date is Thursday, end of day, and I commit to that. If anything changes, you'll hear it from me first.

title: Pitching a small improvement
prompt: Pitch a small process fix to your team. Name the pain, the fix, and the cost.
beats: The headline first: the fix in one line
The reason: the pain it removes
The ask or next step: a one-week trial

skill.answer: A small idea for the team. Right now, every bug report needs three messages before anyone can start, and that friction slows us down. The fix is a five-line template, and it costs ten minutes to set up. Can we run a one-week trial and see if the payoff is real?

title: Escalating without drama
prompt: Escalate an issue stuck for a week. State facts, show attempts, and ask for one decision.
beats: The headline first: what is stuck and since when
The reason: the two things you already tried
The ask or next step: the one decision you need

skill.answer: I need to escalate one item. The data access request has stalled for a week. I've made three attempts, two emails and one call, with no reply. Without it, our testing can't start. Could you decide today: do we go to their head, or do we move the date?

title: Asking to work from home
prompt: Ask to work from home on Friday. Give the reason and show availability stays the same.
beats: The headline first: the day and the request
The reason: why home works better that day
The ask or next step: reachable hours and cover

skill.answer: Could I work from home this Friday? A plumber is coming in the morning, and someone needs to be at home. I'll be available on chat and calls all day, as usual. The deliverable for Friday, the sales deck, will be ready by noon either way.

title: Explaining a missed target
prompt: Explain to your manager why a number was missed. Facts first, then cause, then the fix.
beats: The headline first: the miss in one line
The reason: the one or two real causes
The ask or next step: the fix and next check

skill.answer: We missed the sign-up target: 800 against a goal of 1,000. The main cause was the app store delay; we lost ten days of the campaign. To correct course, we're running the campaign for two extra weeks, starting Monday. I'll share the numbers every Friday.

title: Welcoming a new joiner
prompt: Introduce yourself to a new teammate. Say what you do and offer one concrete help.
beats: The headline first: your role in one line
The reason: what you can help with
The ask or next step: a time to walk them through

skill.answer: Welcome to the team! I'm Fatima, and I handle testing for the mobile app. I'll be your point of contact for anything about releases. Would a thirty-minute walkthrough of our tools tomorrow help? I'll send an invite.

title: Demoing your work in a minute
prompt: Demo what you built in one minute. Show the result first, then one detail, then what is next.
beats: The headline first: what it does now
The reason: the one detail that matters
The ask or next step: what you want feedback on

skill.answer: Here's the outcome first: you can now reorder past purchases in two taps. One detail I like: it remembers your usual delivery slot. Next, we'll test it with fifty users. I'd love your feedback after this demo.

title: Too many tasks at once
prompt: Tell your manager you are overloaded. List the three things and ask which can move.
beats: The headline first: you cannot do all three well
The reason: the three items and their dates
The ask or next step: which one moves

skill.answer: I don't have the bandwidth to finish all three this week: the client deck, the quarterly report and the new joiner's training plan. I can do two of them well. Could you help me prioritise? Which one can move to next week?

title: Following up twice politely
prompt: Follow up a second time on something pending. Stay warm, restate the ask and the date.
beats: The headline first: the pending item
The reason: why the date still matters
The ask or next step: confirm or a new date

skill.answer: Hi Joseph, just a gentle nudge on the access request from last Monday. It's still pending, and we need it by Thursday to start testing. Could you confirm that date works, or let me know who else I should ask?

title: Introducing yourself in 30s
prompt: Introduce yourself to a new client on a call. Name, role, and what you own for them.
beats: The headline first: name and role
The reason: what you own for them
The ask or next step: invite their first concern

skill.answer: Hi, I'm Riya, and I lead your project on our side. I own the delivery plan and the weekly updates. I'm your point of contact, so if you have any concern, big or small, please come straight to me.

title: Giving difficult feedback
prompt: Tell a junior their work needs a rework. Be direct about the gap and kind about the person.
beats: The headline first: the gap in one line
The reason: the standard it missed
The ask or next step: support and a new date

skill.answer: Thanks for the draft. I'll be direct: it needs a rework before it goes to the client. The gap is the numbers; three tables don't match the source. Our standard is that every number is checked twice. You're good at this, and I'll support you: let's go through one table together at three.

title: Requesting a tool or course
prompt: Ask your manager to approve a small tool or course. State cost, benefit, and time needed.
beats: The headline first: what you want approved
The reason: the benefit to the work
The ask or next step: cost and time

skill.answer: Could you approve a short course on data dashboards? The cost is small, and it fits our learning budget. It takes four evenings. The benefit is that I can build our weekly reports myself instead of waiting for the analytics team.

title: Closing a project update
prompt: Close a project review call. Summarise decisions, owners, and the next check-in date.
beats: The headline first: the two decisions taken
The reason: owners against each item
The ask or next step: the next check-in

skill.answer: Let me sum up before we close. Two decisions: we launch on the 15th, and the reports wait for phase two. Owners: Arjun has the launch checklist, and Priya has the client email. Our next check-in is Monday at ten.

title: Chasing a vendor politely
prompt: Chase a vendor who missed a delivery. Firm on the date, polite in tone, clear on impact.
beats: The headline first: the missed date
The reason: the impact on your plan
The ask or next step: the new committed date

skill.answer: Hi, I'm calling about the laptops you committed to deliver last Friday. They haven't arrived. The impact is real: three new joiners start on Monday with nothing to work on. Could you confirm a delivery time for tomorrow?

title: Stating your appraisal case

title: The day results came out

skill.answer: I was at a cyber café with two friends, waiting for the page to load. My hands were cold, and I felt anxious in my stomach. When I saw I'd passed, I didn't feel happy at first. I felt numb, almost blank. Then relief came slowly, like my shoulders dropping. I called my mum, and only when she cried did I start smiling.

title: A friend moving away

beats: The moment: the goodbye itself
What it felt like: the exact feeling underneath
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: I said goodbye to Arjun at the railway station, and we both pretended it was no big deal. On the way home, I felt hollow, as if something normal had just gone missing. Now when I pass our old chai stall, I feel wistful rather than sad. We call every Sunday, and we've managed to stay in touch for two years.

title: Praise you did not expect
prompt: Describe a moment you were praised unexpectedly at work. How did it actually feel?
beats: The moment: who said what and where
What it felt like: the exact feeling
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: In a team call, my manager suddenly said, 'Ravi's report saved us last week.' I felt sheepish at first; my face went warm, and I didn't know where to look. A minute later, I felt validated, as if the late nights had been seen. I left that call motivated and started the next report the same afternoon.

title: Coming home after months
prompt: Describe how you felt walking into your home after months away. What hit you first?
beats: The moment: opening the door
What it felt like: the exact feeling
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: After eight months in another city, I opened the door, and the smell of my mother's cooking hit me first. Everything was so familiar: the creaky fan, the same calendar on the wall. I felt relief first, then I felt grounded, as if my feet were back on solid floor. I sat in the kitchen for an hour, just talking.

title: A rejection that stung
prompt: Describe how you felt after a rejection: a job, a role, or a plan that fell through.
beats: The moment: how you heard the no
What it felt like: the exact feeling, not just sad
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: I got the email on a Monday morning: they'd chosen another candidate. It stung more than I expected, a sharp feeling in my chest, because I'd already pictured myself in that job. For a day, I was crestfallen and quiet. Then I asked them for feedback, used it in my next interview, and bounced back with a better offer a month later.

title: Angry at unfair blame
prompt: Describe a time you were blamed for something that was not your fault. How did it feel?
beats: The moment: the blame landing on you
What it felt like: the exact flavour of anger
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: In a meeting, a senior said the delay was my fault, but I'd sent the file on time. I felt indignant; my ears went hot, and my jaw got tight. It felt deeply unfair. But I kept my voice steady, said, 'Let me share the email,' and showed the time it was sent. He nodded, and we moved on. I was still shaking a little afterwards.

title: Alone in a new city
prompt: Describe your first evening alone in a new city. What did the loneliness feel like?
beats: The moment: the empty room that evening
What it felt like: the exact texture of it
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: My first evening in Hyderabad, I sat on the bed in an empty room with one bag. The silence felt loud. I felt adrift, as if nothing around me belonged to me, and a bit hollow inside. So I went out, found a small dosa place and ate slowly, just to be around people. That's where I started to settle in.

title: Guilt after snapping
prompt: Describe how you felt after snapping at someone you care about. What did the guilt feel like?
beats: The moment: the words leaving your mouth
What it felt like: the guilt afterwards
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: My mum called three times during a busy workday, and I snapped at her: 'I'm working, Mum!' The moment I hung up, I felt remorseful, a heavy, sinking feeling. I couldn't focus for the next hour. So I called her back, apologised properly and asked what she needed. She only wanted to tell me she'd made my favourite dish.

title: Joy that caught you off guard
prompt: Describe a small moment of sudden happiness. What made it different from just feeling good?
beats: The moment: the small trigger
What it felt like: the exact feeling
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: I was walking to the bus stop on a normal Tuesday when a kid on a bicycle waved and shouted, 'Hi, uncle!' I suddenly felt buoyant and light, as if someone had opened a window. It wasn't just feeling good; it came from nowhere. I smiled at strangers all the way to work, and the feeling lingered until lunch.

title: Envy at a friend's win
prompt: Describe feeling envious of a friend's success while still being happy for them. Name both feelings.
beats: The moment: hearing their news
What it felt like: the two feelings side by side
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: My best friend told me she'd got the job in London that I'd also wanted. My happiness for her was genuine; I hugged her right there. But on the way home, I felt a small sting of envy too. I was ambivalent: proud of her and jealous at the same time. So I turned that feeling into drive and signed up for the course I'd been putting off.

title: Nervous before speaking
prompt: Describe how you felt just before speaking in front of a group. Where did you feel it?
beats: The moment: waiting for your turn
What it felt like: the exact physical feeling
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: I was third on the list to present at the team offsite. While the others spoke, I felt jittery; my knee kept bouncing, and I had a dry mouth. I felt it most in my stomach. So I took three slow breaths and drank some water. After my first two sentences, my nerves began to settle.

title: Relief after a health scare
prompt: Describe the relief of hearing good news after a health worry. What did relief feel like?
beats: The moment: the wait before the news
What it felt like: relief arriving in the body
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: My father had some tests, and we waited four days for the results. The whole family was tense; nobody said it, but we all checked our phones too often. When the doctor said everything was normal, I felt my whole body exhale. Relief felt like warm water. I hugged him, and I've felt grateful for ordinary days ever since.

title: Proud of your parents
prompt: Describe a moment you felt proud of your parents. What did they do, and how did pride feel?
beats: The moment: what they did
What it felt like: pride, precisely
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: Last year, my mother finished her degree at fifty-two, studying every night after work. At the ceremony, she walked up in a simple cotton saree. I felt proud, but it was a quiet pride, a warm tightness in my throat, not cheering. I look up to her more than ever, and I tell her that more often now.

title: Bored in a long function
prompt: Describe sitting through a long boring family function. What did the boredom feel like?
beats: The moment: the hour that would not end
What it felt like: boredom in the body
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: At my cousin's engagement, the speeches went on for two hours. The boredom felt physical: I was restless, I kept fidgeting with my phone, and every minute seemed to drag. I counted the lights on the ceiling twice. So I offered to help in the kitchen, and the time finally moved.

title: Hope after a long slump
prompt: Describe the first sign of hope after a long low phase. What changed inside you?
beats: The moment: the small good sign
What it felt like: hope returning
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: For months after losing my job, every day felt grey. Then one morning, a company I liked replied: 'Can we talk this week?' It was only a glimmer, but I felt a lift in my chest, as if I'd been holding my breath. My hope was cautious; I didn't tell anyone yet. But I went for a walk that evening, my first in weeks.

title: Embarrassed in public
prompt: Describe a moment of public embarrassment. What did it feel like, exactly?
beats: The moment: what everyone saw
What it felt like: embarrassment, precisely
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: I tripped on the stairs in a crowded metro station and dropped my lunch box everywhere. Rice on the floor, people staring. I was mortified; my face was burning, and I wanted to disappear. Then an old man picked up my lid and said, 'At least it wasn't biryani.' I laughed it off with him, and the burning went away.

title: Calm on a quiet morning
prompt: Describe a morning when you felt completely calm. What created that calm?
beats: The moment: the morning itself
What it felt like: calm, precisely
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: One Sunday, I woke up before everyone else, made tea and sat on the balcony. No phone, just birds and a slow street. I felt serene and unhurried, as if there was enough time for everything. The calm came from having nothing to answer. After an hour, I had a clarity I never get on weekdays, and I planned my whole week in ten minutes.

title: Too much in one week
prompt: Describe a week when everything piled up at once. What did being overwhelmed feel like?
beats: The moment: the pile-up becoming clear
What it felt like: overwhelm, precisely
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: One week, a client deadline, my sister's wedding preparations and a move to a new flat all landed at once. Feeling overwhelmed was like having too many tabs open in my head; I'd start one thing and jump to another. So on Wednesday, I wrote everything down and did a quick triage. Then I did one thing at a time. The week was still busy, but I could breathe.

title: Missing college days
prompt: Describe missing your college days. What exactly do you miss, and how does it feel?
beats: The moment: what triggered the memory
What it felt like: nostalgia, precisely
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: Sometimes an old song comes on, and I'm back in our hostel corridor at midnight. What I miss isn't the classes. It's how carefree we were: chai at 2 a.m., no calendar, no emails. I feel wistful, a warm ache with a smile in it. So I keep one memory alive: our whole group still meets every December.

title: Confidence after a win
prompt: Describe how real confidence felt after you earned a win. How is it different from showing off?
beats: The moment: the win landing
What it felt like: quiet confidence
What you did next and what stayed with you

skill.answer: After six months of practice, I gave my first client presentation without notes, and it went well. The confidence I felt was quiet. I didn't want to tell everyone; I just felt grounded, steady on my feet. It felt earned, not borrowed. Showing off needs an audience; this didn't. I went home and simply prepared for the next one.

title: Is work from home better?
prompt: Give your view on work from home: is it better than office? Take a side and defend it.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I think a mix is better than full-time office. The main reason is flexibility: I get two hours back on home days, and I use them to work and sleep. The best counterpoint is isolation, and that's real. So I'd keep two office days for people and three home days for focused work. That's the balance.

title: Should cities ban cars?
prompt: Should busy city centres ban private cars? Give your view with one strong reason.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: Yes, I think busy city centres should ban private cars, at least at peak hours. The strongest reason is congestion: too many cars carry just one person and block the road for buses. The best counterpoint is that public transport isn't good enough yet. That's fair, so the ban should come after more buses and metro lines, not before. It's a trade-off worth making.

title: Is ambition overrated?
prompt: Is ambition overrated? Give your view: should people chase big titles or a calm life?
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I don't think ambition is overrated, but chasing titles is. The strongest reason is that ambition for real skills makes work more interesting at any level. The best counterpoint is that ambition has a cost: stress, long hours, less family time. I agree, so I'd aim high on the work I love and stay content with the title I have.

title: Rent or buy a house?
prompt: For a young earner in a big city: is it smarter to rent or buy? Take a clear side.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: For a young earner in a big city, I'd rent. The strongest reason is flexibility: in your twenties, your job and your city can change within a year. The best counterpoint is that rent feels like wasted money. But when I run the numbers, a big loan is a huge commitment that early. So rent now, save, and buy once your life is settled.

title: Are weddings too big?
prompt: Have Indian weddings become too big and wasteful? Give your honest view with a reason.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: Yes, I think many weddings have become too big. The strongest reason is that some families take loans for one weekend, and that's wasteful. The best counterpoint is tradition: weddings bring the whole family together, and that matters. I agree, so I'm for moderation: keep the rituals and the people, and cut the show.

title: Is AI good for jobs?
prompt: Will AI tools create more jobs than they remove? Give your view with one strong reason.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I think AI will change more jobs than it removes. The strongest reason is that it automates tasks, not whole roles, so most people will do the same job with new tools. The best counterpoint is that some jobs will be displaced, especially simple data work. That's true, so companies and people need to adapt early, with real training.

title: Marks or real skills?
prompt: What matters more for a career: high marks or real skills? Take a side and defend it.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I think real skills matter more over a career. The strongest reason is that after your first job, nobody asks about your marks; they ask what you can do. The best counterpoint is that marks are a signal for your first interview. True, so get decent marks, but don't spend years on rote learning when you could build practical skills.

title: Gym or morning walks?
prompt: For staying fit with a desk job: is a gym membership worth it, or are daily walks enough?
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: For most desk workers, I think daily walks are enough to start. The strongest reason is that walking is sustainable; you can stay consistent for years. The best counterpoint is intensity: a gym builds strength that walks don't. That's fair, so I'd walk every day and add two short strength sessions at home.

title: Should you lend to friends?
prompt: Should you lend money to friends? Give your view with the strongest reason behind it.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I'd lend only what I can afford to lose. The strongest reason is the relationship: if money comes between friends, things get awkward fast. The best counterpoint is that friends should help each other. I agree, so I set a clear boundary: a small amount, given freely, and I don't keep asking for it back.

title: Job hop or stay loyal?
prompt: Early in a career: is it better to switch jobs often or stay and grow in one place?
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: Early on, I'd stay in one place for at least two or three years. The strongest reason is growth: you learn more when you see a project from start to finish. The best counterpoint is that switching gives you leverage for a bigger role. True, so switch when the learning stops, not just for the title. Loyalty makes sense only while you're still growing.

title: Metro or your own vehicle?
prompt: In a big Indian city: metro and cabs, or your own two-wheeler? Defend your pick.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: In a big city, I'd pick the metro and cabs. The strongest reason is that the metro is reliable; I know exactly when I'll arrive. The best counterpoint is freedom: with your own two-wheeler, you can go anywhere, any time. That's true, but parking and traffic are a daily hassle. So the metro for work, and a cab when I need the freedom.

title: Early bird or night owl?
prompt: Is waking up early really better, or can night owls be just as sharp? Take a side.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I think night owls can be just as sharp. The strongest reason is that people have different rhythms, and a 5 a.m. alarm makes some of us worse, not better. The best counterpoint is that the early quiet hours are great for focus. True, but the night has quiet hours too. The real myth is that one schedule works for everyone.

title: Eating out every weekend?
prompt: Is eating out every weekend worth the money, or is home food the smarter habit?
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I don't think eating out every weekend is worth it as a habit. The strongest reason is health: restaurant food usually has much more oil and salt than home food. The best counterpoint is that it's how many people relax with friends. Fair, so I'd keep it to twice a month and make it a proper treat.

title: Smartphones: boon or trap?
prompt: Do smartphones help us more than they distract us? Give your view with one strong reason.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I think smartphones help us more than they hurt, if we use them on purpose. The strongest reason is that one tool now handles maps, payments, learning and calls home. The best counterpoint is distraction; most of us check our phones far too often. That's real, so the answer isn't fewer phones; it's more discipline, like no phones at meals.

title: Government job or private?
prompt: For a stable life: a government job or a private one? Give your honest view with a reason.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: For a stable life, I'd choose a private job. The strongest reason is growth: in the private sector, I can learn faster and change roles more easily. The best counterpoint is security; a government job is very hard to lose. That matters, so I'd build my stability from skills and savings instead of the job itself.

title: Reading vs watching videos
prompt: To learn something new: is reading better than watching videos? Defend your pick.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: To learn something deeply, I think reading is better. The strongest reason is depth: I can slow down, reread and think, so I remember more. The best counterpoint is that videos show things words can't, like how to fix a tap. True, so I watch videos for hands-on skills and read for ideas. Watching can feel passive; reading makes me work.

title: Big company or startup?
prompt: Starting out: should a fresher join a big company or a small startup? Take a side.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I'd tell a fresher to join a startup. The strongest reason is learning: you get real responsibility in the first month. The best counterpoint is the brand of a big company and the risk of a startup closing. That's fair, so pick a startup with funding and a good team. Even if it closes, the learning stays with you.

title: Save first or enjoy young?
prompt: In your twenties: save aggressively or spend on experiences? Give your view with a reason.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I'd save first, but not everything. The strongest reason is that savings compound: money you save at twenty-five grows far more than money you save at forty. The best counterpoint is that some experiences only happen when you're young. True, so I'd save a fixed share every month and spend the rest on trips, guilt-free. That's the balance.

title: Small wedding or big one?
prompt: If it were your call: a small wedding or a big celebration? Defend your choice.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: If it were my call, I'd choose a small wedding. The strongest reason is that an intimate wedding lets you actually talk to the people you love. The best counterpoint is family pressure; big celebrations matter a lot to parents. I understand that, so maybe a small wedding and one big dinner. The memory I want is faces, not crowds.

title: English needed for success?
prompt: How much does fluent English matter for success in India? Give your honest view.
beats: Your view in one line
The strongest reason behind it
The best counterpoint and your answer to it

skill.answer: I think fluent English is a door-opener in India, but it isn't success by itself. The strongest reason is that interviews, client calls and most office emails happen in English. The best counterpoint is that many people succeed in business without it. True, so I see English as one skill among many. What it really gives you is confidence in the room.

title: Where I grew up
prompt: Tell someone where you grew up. Paint the place in two lines, then what it gave you.

What happened there: one memory that captures it
What it changed: what you carried from it

skill.answer: I grew up in a small neighbourhood in Indore, in a lane where every door stayed open in the evenings. You could smell three kitchens at once. One summer, the whole lane chipped in to fix the roof of the old man next door. That's what shaped me: I learnt that neighbours are family. My roots are in that lane, wherever I live.

title: A teacher who mattered
prompt: Tell someone about a teacher who changed you. What did they do that others did not?
beats: Where and when: the class and the teacher
What happened: the one thing they did
What it changed: how you are different for it

skill.answer: In class nine, our maths teacher, Mrs Thomas, was the strictest in school. I was failing, and I'd stopped trying. But one day she kept me after class and said, 'You're not bad at maths. You're scared of it.' She believed in me before I did. That was the turning point. I scored ninety that year, and I still say that kind of thing to juniors.

title: A decision that changed me
prompt: Tell someone about one decision that changed your direction. What were the options?
beats: Where and when: the choice in front of you
What happened: what you picked and why
What it changed: where it led

skill.answer: After my engineering degree, I was at a crossroads. I had a safe job offer from a big IT company and a place on a design course in Ahmedabad. My parents wanted the job. But I kept picturing myself sketching, not coding. So I took the gamble and chose the course, with a loan and a lot of worry. Today I design apps for a living. It wasn't easy, but I have no regrets.

title: What my father taught me
prompt: Tell someone the most important thing your father taught you, with one real example.
beats: Where and when: the example you remember
What happened: what he did or said
What it changed: how you use it today

skill.answer: The most important thing my father taught me was to keep your word. He believed in discipline, but he never lectured; he taught by example. When I was ten, he promised a neighbour he'd help him move house on a Sunday. That morning, he had a high fever, but he still went, slowly carrying the light boxes. I live by that now: if I say I'll do something, I do it.

title: What my mother taught me
prompt: Tell someone the most important thing your mother taught you, with one real example.
beats: Where and when: the example you remember
What happened: what she did or said
What it changed: how you use it today

skill.answer: My mother taught me that warmth costs nothing. When I was in school, she fed every friend who came home, even when money was tight. Once, she packed an extra tiffin every day for a boy whose mother was ill. I only understood that sacrifice years later. I try to carry it forward: there's always a seat at my table.

title: My biggest failure so far
prompt: Tell someone about your biggest failure. Be honest about your part in it.
beats: Where and when: what you attempted
What happened: how it fell apart and your part
What it changed: what you do differently now

skill.answer: My biggest failure was my first startup, a food delivery app in Pune. We had a good team and some early users. But I spent all my time on the app and almost none talking to restaurants. I have to own that part. After eight months, the money ran out, and we shut it down. Telling my parents was humbling. The lesson stayed: talk to the people you serve before you build.

title: My first day at work
prompt: Tell someone about your first day at your first job. What do you still remember?
beats: Where and when: the office and the morning
What happened: the moments that stuck
What it changed: what that day taught you

skill.answer: My first job was at a bank in Chennai. On the first day, I wore new shoes that hurt and arrived forty minutes early. I was nervous and completely clueless about the systems. But at lunch, an older colleague, Joseph, sat with me and said, 'Ask me anything, even silly things.' That welcome changed everything. I still do the same for every new joiner.

title: My oldest friendship
prompt: Tell someone about your oldest friend. How did you meet, and why did it last?
beats: Where and when: how you met
What happened: one memory that defines it
What it changed: what the friendship gave you

skill.answer: My oldest friend is Sameer. We met in class two, when he shared his lunch because I'd forgotten mine. Twenty years later, he's still the first person I call. When my dad was in hospital, Sameer slept in the waiting room for three nights without being asked. That's why it lasted: he's loyal, through thick and thin. Our bond is that simple.

title: Moving to a new city
prompt: Tell someone about moving to a new city. What was hardest, and what surprised you?
beats: Where and when: the move itself
What happened: the hardest part first
What it changed: what the city made of you

skill.answer: I moved from Lucknow to Bengaluru at twenty-two for my first job. The hardest part was the first month; I felt adrift, eating alone and not knowing anyone. But what surprised me was how quickly I learnt to cook, pay bills and fix things myself. It took about six months to settle in. The move made me independent in a way home never could.

title: My first salary
prompt: Tell someone about your first salary. How much did it matter, and what did you do with it?
beats: Where and when: the job and roughly what it paid
What happened: what you did with it
What it changed: what earning taught you

skill.answer: My first salary arrived on a Friday evening, and I checked my bank app about ten times. It wasn't a big amount, but it was the first money I'd earned myself, and I was so proud. I took my parents out to dinner and bought my dad a watch. He still wears it. That day taught me the value of money better than any advice.

title: A habit I finally broke
prompt: Tell someone about a bad habit you finally broke. What worked when nothing else did?

skill.answer: For years, I scrolled on my phone in bed until one in the morning. I tried deleting apps, but nothing lasted. Then I noticed the trigger: I picked up the phone the moment I lay down. So I started leaving it to charge in the kitchen and replaced it with a paper book. The first week was hard. Now I'm on a ninety-day streak, and I'm asleep by eleven.

title: Someone who believed in me
prompt: Tell someone about a person who believed in you before you believed in yourself.

What it changed: what you dared after that

skill.answer: In my first job, I was a junior who never spoke in meetings. My manager, Priya, saw potential that I didn't. One day she said, 'You're presenting the client update on Friday.' I panicked, but she gave me her backing and practised with me twice. It went well. I can't really repay her, so I try to do the same for my own juniors.

title: My college years in a minute

skill.answer: I studied commerce at a college in Delhi. We were always broke and completely carefree. My favourite memory is the night before an exam when the power went out, and ten of us studied by one torch, laughing more than reading. I walked in shy and walked out able to talk to anyone. Those were my most formative years.

title: The biggest risk I took
prompt: Tell someone about the biggest risk you ever took. What was at stake?

skill.answer: Three years ago, I left a stable job to join a five-person startup. The stakes were real: a smaller salary, a home loan and my parents' worry. But I'd stopped learning at the old job. So I took the leap. The first year was hard; we nearly ran out of money twice. But I learnt more in that one year than in the five before it. It was worth it.

title: Growing up with siblings

skill.answer: I grew up with an older brother, and our rivalry was serious, especially over the TV remote. Once we fought so hard over cricket that we broke Mum's favourite vase. But then we did something new: we teamed up, glued it together and hid the crack behind a photo. She found out a year later and laughed. That's our bond: we fight, then we fix things together.

title: A trip that changed me
prompt: Tell someone about a trip that changed how you see things. Where did you go?

What it changed: what you see differently now

skill.answer: Two years ago, I went to Spiti with two friends. We'd planned every day, but a landslide closed the road, and we were stuck in a small village for three days. A family there gave us food and blankets and wouldn't take anything in return. I was humbled. That trip changed my perspective: now I travel with fewer plans, wander more and notice people more.

title: Learning something hard

skill.answer: At twenty-eight, I decided to learn to swim. The first month was embarrassing; kids half my size were faster. Then I hit a plateau: for six weeks, I couldn't swim more than one length. But I kept going, three mornings a week, and my coach kept saying, 'Slow down. Breathe.' One day, I just did four lengths. The payoff was bigger than swimming: I learnt that if I persist, I get there.

title: The house I grew up in

skill.answer: I grew up in an old house in Kochi with a small courtyard in the middle. The room I remember most is the kitchen, with the aroma of coconut oil and curry leaves every morning. The sound I remember is the echo of June rain on the tin roof over the courtyard. Even today, when I smell curry leaves, I'm ten years old again.

title: Why I chose this career

skill.answer: I didn't plan this career; I stumbled into it. I'd studied mechanical engineering, but in my final year, I helped a friend build a website for his shop, and I loved it. So I took a short coding course and applied for junior developer jobs. Six years later, I lead a small team. I wouldn't call it a calling, but I have no regrets.

title: Festivals at my home

skill.answer: At our home in Kolkata, Durga Puja was everything. For five days, the house was full of bustle: cousins arriving, aunts cooking, and my grandmother counting the sweets so nobody ate them early. Every evening, we walked together from pandal to pandal until our feet hurt. What I still carry from it is the togetherness, more than the lights or the food.

skill.answer: The best advice I ever got was from my first manager, Arjun: 'Write it down before you say it.' It stuck with me. It proved true two years later, in a tense meeting with an angry client. I'd written three points on paper, so I stayed calm and clear while everyone else argued. Now I live by it before every important call.

title: The toughest year so far

skill.answer: My toughest year was 2020. I lost my job in April, and my father was unwell for most of the year. Some days I didn't want to get out of bed. What got me through was learning to lean on people: my sister called every night, and an old friend found me freelance work. By December, I had a new job. I emerged more resilient, and much better at asking for help.

skill.answer: In five years, I want to lead a small product team in Pune, close to my parents. I'm already working towards it: my first milestone is to run one project from start to finish by next year. Outside work, I want to run a half marathon and have a flat with a balcony full of plants. Concrete goals give me purpose; vague ones never did.

title: A school memory I love

skill.answer: In class eight, my gang of four hid the teacher's attendance register as a joke. But the principal walked in looking for it, and we panicked. So we confessed, and he made us clean the library for a week. It turned into the best week of school: we read comics behind the shelves. That bit of mischief still fills me with nostalgia.

title: My story in two minutes
prompt: Tell a new friend your life story in two minutes: where from, what shaped you, where headed.

skill.answer: I'm from Nagpur. That's where my roots are: a joint family, a busy house, and parents who ran a small medical shop. I studied engineering because everyone did. The turning point came in my first job, when I gave a client demo and loved it more than the coding. So I moved into product roles. Now I live in Bengaluru, and I'm headed towards building my own product one day.
